pos: interj. (Aramaic, my God; the first word of Christ's cry from the cross in Mark)
etymology: Aramaic Elahi, my God, from Elah, God, answering to the Hebrew Eli of Psalm 22:1; named once, Mark 15:34.
biblical_def: Eloi is the first word of the fourth saying from the cross as Mark records it: “And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani? which is, being interpreted, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34). Matthew gives the same cry in the Hebrew form: “Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?” (Matthew 27:46). The words are a quotation. They are the opening of the twenty-second Psalm: “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?” (Psalm 22:1). Our Lord, in the hour of the curse, spoke Scripture. The darkness had been over the whole land from the sixth hour to the ninth, and at the end of it He cried out the one text that had described His death a thousand years before it happened. The cry is not despair and not a loss of faith — the possessive holds: my God. It is the voice of the Son bearing the wrath of God in the place of His people, forsaken in the judicial sense while never ceasing to be the beloved Son. The word Eloi is a window into the atonement: God addressed as God by One who was being treated as sin.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Eloi, Aramaic for my God; the first word of Christ's cry from the cross as recorded at Mark 15:34, quoting Psalm 22:1.

And when the sixth hour was come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour.
corruption_summary: The cry is read as Jesus losing faith or as the Father abandoning the Son in His being; Scripture presents a judicial forsaking borne by One who still says my God.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors meet at this verse. Liberal theology takes the cry as evidence that Jesus died disillusioned, a good man who discovered at the end that God was not there — which requires ignoring that the sentence is a quotation He chose. The opposite error, found in some popular preaching, speaks as though the Trinity were broken on the cross and the Son ceased to be loved by the Father. Neither will stand. The eternal relations of the Persons are immutable; what the Son bore was the penal abandonment due to His people, the hiding of God's favour from the sin-bearer, not a rupture in the Godhead.

The Authorized Version keeps the Aramaic and then translates it, which is itself a defence against both errors: Mark wants the reader to hear the actual syllables and to know exactly what they mean. Christ was made a curse for us, and the cry is what the curse sounded like in the mouth of the sinless. The Reformed doctrine of penal substitution is not read into Mark 15:34; it is the only reading that accounts for both halves of the verse — forsaken, and still my God.

pos: n. (the faithful martyr of Pergamos, commended by Christ)
etymology: Greek Antipas, a contraction of Antipater, for the father, or in place of the father; named once, Revelation 2:13.
biblical_def: Antipas is named once, and the one who names him is the risen Christ: “I know thy works, and where thou dwellest, even where Satan's seat is: and thou holdest fast my name, and hast not denied my faith, even in those days wherein Antipas was my faithful martyr, who was slain among you, where Satan dwelleth” (Revelation 2:13). Of his life nothing is recorded. He is identified entirely by his death and by the One he died for — my faithful martyr. Pergamos was the seat of the imperial cult in Asia, the first city of the province to raise a temple to Rome and Augustus, and it is to that city that Christ says Satan's seat is there. Antipas died in it. The letter to Pergamos goes on to rebuke the church for tolerating the doctrine of Balaam and the doctrine of the Nicolaitans, so the congregation that produced a martyr was also a congregation making peace with error. Both things are said to the same church. The promise held out to the overcomer in that letter is the hidden manna and a white stone with a new name written. This Antipas is not Herod Antipas the tetrarch; the two are distinct men who share a common Greek name.

corruption_summary: Martyrdom is recast as fanaticism and faithfulness as intolerance; Christ names a dead man His own and rebukes the surviving church for its tolerance of error.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern instinct is to admire the martyr while declining his convictions, and to treat doctrinal firmness as the thing that gets people killed unnecessarily. The letter to Pergamos refuses that separation. Christ commends Antipas for holding fast His name and not denying His faith, and in the next breath He rebukes the church for having them that hold the doctrine of Balaam and the doctrine of the Nicolaitans. Faithfulness unto death and intolerance of false teaching are the same virtue in the same letter.

A church may contain a martyr and a heresy at once; that is the sober lesson of Pergamos, and it is the reason the dictionary holds the line on doctrine. The Nicolaitans taught a liberty that dissolved into fornication and idol-meat, which is the ancient form of the progressive accommodation now urged on the churches. Antipas died rather than confess Caesar, and the congregation he died among was quietly conceding to the spirit of the city. Christ says both.

pos: n. (the man to whom Luke addressed his Gospel and the Acts)
etymology: Greek Theophilos, loved of God, or friend of God, from theos, God, and philos, loving; named twice, Luke 1:3 and Acts 1:1.
biblical_def: Theophilus is the man to whom both of Luke's books are addressed: “It seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order, most excellent Theophilus” (Luke 1:3), and again at the opening of the second volume, “The former treatise have I made, O Theophilus, of all that Jesus began both to do and teach” (Acts 1:1). Nothing else is known of him. The title most excellent is the form of address used in the Acts for Roman officials, which has long suggested a man of rank; the name means loved of God. Luke states his purpose to him plainly: “That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed” (Luke 1:4). Theophilus had already been taught, and Luke wrote so that he might have certainty — a researched, ordered, eyewitness-sourced account set down in writing. The two longest books in the New Testament exist because one man needed to be sure. That is the dictionary's own warrant for existing. This Theophilus is not Theophilus of Antioch, the second-century apologist and bishop who wrote to Autolycus; they are two men a century apart who share a common Greek name.

corruption_summary: The Gospels are treated as community folklore; Luke names his method, his sources, his purpose and his reader in four opening verses.
corruption_paragraphs: Form criticism built a century of scholarship on the premise that the Gospels grew out of anonymous community tradition rather than being composed by authors working from testimony. Luke's preface is the standing refutation. He says that many had taken the work in hand, that the matters were delivered by them which from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word, that he had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, that he wrote in order, and that he wrote to a named man so that man could know the certainty of what he had been taught. That is not folklore; it is a stated historical method with a dedicatee.

The second corruption is the devotional one that dissolves Theophilus into a symbol — any lover of God, the reader himself. The name does mean loved of God, and the application is fair enough as application, but the text addresses a person, with an honorific proper to office, in the manner of ancient dedications. Scripture's certainty is historical before it is experiential: “that thou mightest know the certainty” is written to a man who could be asked.

pos: n. (daughter of Joram, wife of Jehoiada, who hid the infant Joash from Athaliah)
etymology: Hebrew Yehosheba, the LORD is an oath, or Jehovah hath sworn, from Yeho, for Jehovah, with shaba, to swear; called Jehoshabeath in 2 Chronicles 22:11.
biblical_def: Jehosheba saved the line of David: “But Jehosheba, the daughter of king Joram, sister of Ahaziah, took Joash the son of Ahaziah, and stole him from among the king's sons which were slain; and they hid him, even him and his nurse, in the bedchamber from Athaliah, so that he was not slain” (2 Kings 11:2). The Chronicler gives her name in its longer form, Jehoshabeath, and adds that she was the wife of Jehoiada the priest. Athaliah, her own stepmother, had destroyed all the seed royal in order to reign, and the house of David came down to one baby in a priest's keeping: “And he was with her hid in the house of the LORD six years. And Athaliah did reign over the land” (2 Kings 11:3). Six years the rightful king of Judah was an infant hidden in the temple while a usurper sat on his throne, and the whole promise of a son of David on that throne forever hung on a woman's nerve and a nurse's silence. Her name means Jehovah hath sworn. The LORD had sworn to David that he would not lack a man to sit on his throne, and the oath was kept, that generation, by Jehosheba.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Jehosheba, daughter of king Joram and wife of Jehoiada the priest, who hid the infant Joash from Athaliah; called Jehoshabeath in Chronicles.
webster_full: Hebrew Yehosheba, the LORD is an oath, or Jehovah hath sworn.

Once have I sworn by my holiness that I will not lie unto David.
corruption_summary: Women in Scripture are said to be passive or erased; the Davidic line survived one generation because a woman stole a baby out of a massacre.
corruption_paragraphs: Feminist readings of the Old Testament insist that its women are silenced, and complementarian conviction is said to require it. Both claims founder on chapters like this one. Scripture names Jehosheba, states her parentage, her marriage, and her act, and makes the survival of the messianic line depend on it. Nothing in the complementarian position minimises such courage; the biblical order of headship in home and church has never meant that women do not act decisively, and the text of 2 Kings 11 is one of the places where everything turns on a woman's obedience.

Set against her is Athaliah, the only woman to reign over Judah, who seized the throne by murdering her own grandchildren. The chapter gives both: a woman who took power by destroying the seed royal, and a woman who preserved it by hiding one child for six years. The principle to recover is that God's promises are kept through ordinary faithfulness in appalling circumstances, and that the oath sworn to David — “his seed shall endure for ever” — was never at the mercy of Athaliah.

pos: n. (mother of king Jehoiakim of Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Zebuddah, given, or endowed, from zabad, to bestow or to endow; named once, 2 Kings 23:36.
biblical_def: Zebudah is named once, in the formula with which the book of Kings opens the reign of every king of Judah: “Jehoiakim was twenty and five years old when he began to reign; and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Zebudah, the daughter of Pedaiah of Rumah” (2 Kings 23:36). The queen mother is named for every Judahite king, and the notice is never idle; in a kingdom where the mother of the king held real standing, the historian records whose house she came from. The verdict on her son follows at once: “And he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to all that his fathers had done” (2 Kings 23:37). Jehoiakim is the king who cut Jeremiah's scroll with a penknife and burned it leaf by leaf on the hearth, who shed innocent blood, and of whom Jeremiah prophesied that he should be buried with the burial of an ass. His father was Josiah, the best king since David. Zebudah's name means given. She was a daughter of Rumah given to the most faithful king of the later monarchy, and the son she bore undid his father's reformation inside a decade.

corruption_summary: Godly parentage is treated as a guarantee of godly children; Josiah's reformation did not pass to Josiah's sons, and Scripture records the fact without softening it.
corruption_paragraphs: A great deal of family-ministry teaching rests on the premise that faithful parenting secures faithful children, with Proverbs 22:6 pressed into service as a promise. Josiah is the case that will not fit. No king since David was more thorough in reform — the high places broken, the book of the law read in the hearing of all the people, the Passover kept as it had not been kept since the days of the judges — and his son Jehoiakim burned the word of God in a brazier and filled Jerusalem with innocent blood.

The principle to recover is that regeneration is monergistic and does not run in the blood. Covenant households are a great mercy and the ordinary place of conversion, and they are not a mechanism. “Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” settles the matter in John 1:13. Zebudah's name means given; what was given to her was a son who hated the Scriptures, and the fault lay in him.

pos: n. (a Levite who weighed the temple vessels brought back from Babylon)
etymology: Hebrew No'adyah, the LORD hath met, or Jehovah hath assembled, from ya'ad, to appoint or to meet; named once as this man, Ezra 8:33.
biblical_def: Noadiah the Levite was one of four men who received and weighed the silver, the gold and the vessels of the house of God when Ezra's company reached Jerusalem: “Now on the fourth day was the silver and the gold and the vessels weighed in the house of our God by the hand of Meremoth the son of Uriah the priest; and with him was Eleazar the son of Phinehas; and with them was Jozabad the son of Jeshua, and Noadiah the son of Binnui, Levites” (Ezra 8:33). The weighing matters. Ezra had refused a military escort from the king, having told him that the hand of our God is upon all them for good that seek him, and had then carried the temple treasure four months across open country on that confession alone. He had weighed it out to twelve priests at the start and he weighed it in on arrival, so that every talent could be accounted for. Noadiah held one end of that audit. His name means the LORD hath met. The man is distinct from the prophetess Noadiah whom Nehemiah names among those that would have put him in fear a century later — a different person, of the opposite tendency, who happens to bear the same name.

corruption_summary: Faith is set against prudence as though trusting God excluded keeping accounts; Ezra refused an escort and weighed every vessel twice.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors are corrected by this chapter. The first is the presumption that calls recklessness faith: Ezra did decline the king's soldiers, but he did so having proclaimed a fast and sought God about it, and he did not thereby abandon care for what he carried. The second is the worldly prudence that treats stewardship as a substitute for dependence. Ezra did both — no escort, and a double weighing with named witnesses and everything written down.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that financial integrity in the house of God is a spiritual duty, not an administrative afterthought. Paul kept the same practice with the collection for Judea, sending men chosen by the churches so that no man should blame him in that abundance. Noadiah the Levite is remembered for standing at a scale, and the ministry that will not stand at a scale has already failed.

pos: n. (father of the Zacharias whose blood Christ names as the last of the martyrs)
etymology: Greek Barachias, for the Hebrew Berekyah, blessed of the LORD, from barak, to bless, with Yah; named once, Matthew 23:35.
biblical_def: Barachias is named once, and only as a father, in the most severe passage our Lord ever spoke: “That upon you may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel unto the blood of Zacharias son of Barachias, whom ye slew between the temple and the altar” (Matthew 23:35). The sentence closes the woes against the scribes and Pharisees. Christ draws a line from the first murder in Scripture to the last one in the Hebrew order of the books, and charges the whole of it on that generation. The Zacharias in view is the priest stoned in the court of the house of the LORD at the commandment of king Joash — the man whose dying words were, The LORD look upon it, and require it. The Chronicler calls him the son of Jehoiada; Matthew calls him the son of Barachias, which is readily explained if Barachias were a further ancestor or a second name in the family, as double naming is common in the record. What the verse establishes is the unity of the witness: from Abel to Zacharias, the blood of the righteous has one accounting, and the Lord Himself keeps the ledger.

corruption_summary: Christ's woes are explained away as later anti-Jewish polemic; they are a prophet's indictment of the leaders of His own people, spoken in the temple before He wept over the city.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 23 is routinely handled as a late insertion reflecting the hostility of a post-war church rather than the words of Jesus. Two things in the chapter resist it. The woes are spoken by a Jew to Jewish leaders in the Jewish temple, in the exact register of Jeremiah and Amos against the rulers of Israel — prophetic indictment from inside the covenant, not polemic from outside it. And they end in tears: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often would I have gathered thy children together, and ye would not.

The passage has also been abused in the other direction, as warrant for hatred of the Jewish people. That is forbidden by the text itself, which closes with Christ's lament over the city He was about to die for, and by Paul, whose heart's desire and prayer to God for Israel was that they might be saved. The principle to recover is that God requires the blood of His righteous ones, that He requires it of those actually guilty, and that the One who pronounced the woes went from the temple to the cross.

pos: n. (the father whose sons built the fish gate in Nehemiah's wall)
etymology: Hebrew Hassena'ah, the thorn-hedge, or possibly the Senaah with the article prefixed; named once, Nehemiah 3:3.
biblical_def: Hassenaah is named once, and his sons are the ones who did the work: “But the fish gate did the sons of Hassenaah build, who also laid the beams thereof, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof” (Nehemiah 3:3). Nehemiah 3 is the register of the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem, and it is one of the most practical chapters in Scripture: it goes around the circuit of the city gate by gate and names who repaired each stretch — the high priest and his brethren, the men of Jericho, the goldsmiths, the apothecaries, the rulers of districts, the daughters of Shallum, and the sons of Hassenaah at the fish gate. The detail descends to beams, doors, locks and bars. Nothing about this is incidental. The wall was built in fifty-two days under armed threat, every man with his sword girded at his side, because Sanballat and Tobiah had laughed at them and then conspired against them. The record names the households who did the work so that the city would know, and so that we would. The sons of Hassenaah hung the doors of one gate, and Scripture kept their father's name for it.

corruption_summary: Ordinary labour is thought unspiritual beside preaching and prayer; Nehemiah 3 is a chapter of Scripture devoted to naming who hung which door.
corruption_paragraphs: The sacred-secular divide is a standing corruption in the church, and Nehemiah 3 is written against it. An entire chapter of inspired Scripture consists of the names of families and the sections of masonry they repaired, down to the ironmongery of a single gate. The men holding trowels were doing the work of God as truly as Ezra reading the law two chapters later, and Nehemiah's own account has them working with one hand and holding a weapon with the other.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity and the record of ordinary work done in faith. “Whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” is the New Testament form of the same doctrine. A man may be remembered in the word of God solely because his sons set the locks and the bars on one gate of Jerusalem, and that is honour enough.

pos: n. (a Levite sent by Jehoshaphat to teach the law in the cities of Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Tob'adoniyah, good is my Lord Jehovah, from tob, good, adon, lord, and Yah; named once, 2 Chronicles 17:8.
biblical_def: Tobadonijah is the last-named of the nine Levites Jehoshaphat commissioned to teach: “And with them he sent Levites, even Shemaiah, and Nethaniah, and Zebadiah, and Asahel, and Shemiramoth, and Jehonathan, and Adonijah, and Tobijah, and Tobadonijah, Levites; and with them Elishama and Jehoram, priests” (2 Chronicles 17:8). Their work is described in the next verse: “And they taught in Judah, and had the book of the law of the LORD with them, and went about throughout all the cities of Judah, and taught the people” (2 Chronicles 17:9). This is the first recorded itinerant teaching mission in Scripture — a king in the third year of his reign sending princes, Levites and priests circuit-riding through his kingdom with the Scriptures in hand, to teach the people. The result is recorded plainly: the fear of the LORD fell upon the kingdoms round about, and they made no war against Jehoshaphat. His name is a whole confession: good is my Lord Jehovah. Nothing else is said of him. He was one of nine men who carried the book of the law from town to town, and that commission is the ancestor of every faithful pulpit since.

And the fear of the LORD fell upon all the kingdoms of the lands that were round about Judah, so that they made no war against Jehoshaphat.
corruption_summary: Teaching is treated as one ministry option among many; Jehoshaphat's reform began by sending men with the book of the law into every city.
corruption_paragraphs: Where the modern church seeks renewal it reaches first for method, music, and management. Jehoshaphat reached for teachers and a book. The text is explicit that they had the book of the law of the LORD with them, that they went about throughout all the cities, and that they taught the people — and the chapter attributes the kingdom's subsequent peace and strength to it. Reformation follows the opened Scriptures, as it did under Josiah, under Ezra, and in the sixteenth century.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the ordinary means of grace — the word preached and taught, the ordinances, prayer — are what God has appointed to build His people, and that nothing substitutes for them. Nine Levites, two priests, five princes and one book turned a kingdom. The man named Good-is-my-Lord-Jehovah was one of the nine, and the record of his life is that he taught.

pos: n. (a priest's son with a musical instrument at the dedication of the wall)
etymology: Hebrew Ma'ai, compassionate, or possibly a contraction of a longer name in Yah; named once, Nehemiah 12:36.
biblical_def: Maai stands in the company of musicians at the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem: “And his brethren, Shemaiah, and Azarael, Milalai, Gilalai, Maai, Nethaneel, and Judah, Hanani, with the musical instruments of David the man of God, and Ezra the scribe before them” (Nehemiah 12:36). The occasion is the great day of Nehemiah 12, when two companies of singers went in procession along the top of the wall in opposite directions, met at the house of God, and the joy of Jerusalem was heard afar off. Maai carried one of the musical instruments of David the man of God — the phrase is the chapter's own, and it matters: the instruments and the orders of the singers went back to David's appointment, and the restored city reached back five hundred years to resume the worship he had arranged. Ezra the scribe walked before them. Nothing else is recorded of Maai. He is one of eight men named in a single verse because they played at the dedication, and the record of his life in the word of God is that he was there with an instrument when Jerusalem sang.

scriptures: And his brethren, Shemaiah, and Azarael, Milalai, Gilalai, Maai, Nethaneel, and Judah, Hanani, with the musical instruments of David the man of God, and Ezra the scribe before them.

And at the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem they sought the Levites out of all their places, to bring them to Jerusalem, to keep the dedication with gladness, both with thanksgivings, and with singing, with cymbals, psalteries, and with harps.

Also that day they offered great sacrifices, and rejoiced: for God had made them rejoice with great joy: the wives also and the children rejoiced: so that the joy of Jerusalem was heard even afar off.

corruption_summary: Worship music is treated as a matter of taste and innovation; Nehemiah's restored city went back to the instruments and orders David had appointed.
corruption_paragraphs: Debates over music in worship generally proceed as questions of preference and effectiveness. Nehemiah 12 proceeds differently. The singers are gathered by their genealogies, the Levites are purified, the instruments are specified as the musical instruments of David the man of God, and the orders of service are traced to David and Solomon. The restored community did not design a liturgy; it resumed one. That is the regulative instinct applied to praise.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that joy in worship and order in worship are not rivals. The same chapter that records the appointed instruments and the purified Levites also says that they offered great sacrifices and rejoiced, for God had made them rejoice with great joy, and the joy of Jerusalem was heard even afar off. Maai was one of the men making that sound, under David's arrangement, by Nehemiah's appointment, with Ezra walking in front.
